Why Field Notes Beat Memory

Field researchers learn early that memory is a poor instrument. A bird seen at dawn becomes, by evening, a bird that might have been seen at dawn, and by the next week it has merged with every other bird of the same color. The fix is not a better memory. It is a notebook opened at the moment of observation, with the time, the place, the weather, and what was actually seen, written before any interpretation gets added on top.

The same discipline works far from the field. A meeting recorded in the room reads differently from one reconstructed on the train home. The reconstruction is smoother and more confident, and it is usually wrong in small ways that matter later. Writing in the moment feels slower, and the notes look rough, but rough notes that are true beat polished notes that drift. The rest of this piece looks at how working scientists structure a page so that it stays useful for decades, starting with the header line that every entry gets before anything else is written.
